Name: Climate Cycles
Description: Long-term naturally occurring climate fluctuations — glacial and interglacial periods — that are part of Earth's natural rhythm, not driven by human activity. Example: 'The climate has always changed naturally throughout history.'

Name: Solar Activity & Orbital Changes
Description: Variations in solar radiation and Earth's orbital patterns (Milankovitch cycles) that naturally influence global temperatures over thousands of years. Example: 'The Sun's cycles are the primary drivers of climate fluctuations.'

Name: Volcanic Activity
Description: Volcanic eruptions releasing greenhouse gases and aerosols into the atmosphere, affecting global temperatures over short and long time frames. Example: 'Volcanic eruptions release large amounts of CO₂ and aerosols, affecting global temperatures.'

Name: Ocean Cycles
Description: Shifts in ocean currents and naturally occurring oceanic phenomena like El Niño, La Niña, and AMOC that redistribute heat globally and influence climate variability. Example: 'El Niño and La Niña significantly alter weather patterns and global temperatures.'

Name: Geological & Plate Tectonic Movements
Description: Long-term geological processes such as continental drift and plate tectonics that alter ocean currents and atmospheric circulation over millions of years. Example: 'Continental drift and tectonic shifts alter ocean currents and atmospheric circulation.'

Name: Greenhouse Gases
Description: Role of CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O in driving climate change through human activities; atmospheric pollution intensifying the greenhouse effect. Includes: ozone, gases trapped in air, heat-trapping gases. Excludes: general pollution (e.g., 'there is a lot of pollution'). Example: 'Increasing greenhouse gases are warming the planet.'

Name: Overproduction & Unsustainable Output Pressure
Description: Systemic industrial and economic practices maximising profit and output, surpassing social and ecological needs; embedded in global supply chains and market pressures beyond individual control. Example: 'The Industrial Revolution marked the beginning of rapid CO₂ accumulation in the atmosphere.'

Name: Energy Production & Fossil Fuel Dependency
Description: Large-scale energy production and extraction systems (oil drilling, coal mining, power plants, refineries, national energy grids) as structural drivers of climate change. Excludes: end-use fossil fuel consumption by individuals. Example: 'Burning fossil fuels releases CO₂, the primary driver of global warming.'

Name: Industries and Industrial Processes
Description: Industrial activity, machinery, factories, and emissions from chemical and manufacturing processes (cement, steel, fertilizers, refrigerants) releasing CO₂ and other greenhouse gases. Example: 'Industrial pollution is worsening air quality and accelerating climate change.'

Name: Overexploitation of Ecosystems & Land Use Changes
Description: Large-scale transformation and degradation of natural ecosystems — deforestation, wetland drainage, grassland conversion, intensive mining, marine exploitation — reducing carbon sinks. Example: 'Cutting down trees reduces the planet's ability to absorb CO₂.'

Name: Agriculture & Livestock Farming
Description: Emissions-heavy agricultural processes: methane from animal digestion and manure, nitrous oxide from fertilizers, and carbon emissions from land conversion for crops and grazing. Example: 'Intensive livestock farming is a major source of methane, a powerful greenhouse gas.'

Name: Military Emissions & Warfare
Description: Heavy environmental footprint of military training, operations, infrastructure, and conflict-related destruction, often unregulated or unaccounted for in international climate agreements. Example: 'Military carbon footprints are exempt from climate treaties, masking their true impact.'

Name: Unsustainable Consumerism & Overconsumption
Description: Demand for consumer goods (clothing, electronics, packaging, single-use plastic) requiring resource-intensive production; fast fashion, planned obsolescence, and digital culture contributing to emissions and waste. Example: 'Fast fashion and global supply chains contribute to a massive carbon footprint.'

Name: Dietary Choices
Description: Consumption of food products — particularly meat, dairy, and imported goods — with a disproportionately high carbon footprint due to land use, water consumption, and methane emissions. Example: 'High meat and dairy consumption increases greenhouse gas emissions.'

Name: Household Energy Choices
Description: Personal domestic choices increasing energy use and carbon emissions: gas heating systems, poorly insulated homes, high electricity consumption, inefficient appliances. Example: 'Heating and cooling homes consumes a lot of energy and emits CO₂.'

Name: Transportation Choices
Description: Individuals' transportation preferences — reliance on private vehicles, non-electric cars, frequent flying — contributing significantly to CO₂ emissions in car-dependent societies. Example: 'Our dependence on cars instead of public transport is worsening urban pollution and emissions.'

Name: Waste Production & Management
Description: How individuals generate and handle waste (organic and plastic): excessive food waste, limited recycling, reliance on landfill-bound packaging contributing to methane emissions. Example: 'Decomposing organic waste in landfills releases methane into the atmosphere.'

Name: Governmental Inaction in Climate Regulations
Description: Lack of strong enforceable environmental policies and failure to implement international agreements; perceived inability or unwillingness of governments to act decisively due to political short-termism. Example: 'Governments fail to enforce strong environmental laws, allowing pollution to continue.'

Name: Lack of Low-Impact Transportation Systems
Description: Absence or insufficiency of sustainable transport infrastructure investments (public transit, bike lanes, pedestrian-friendly planning); urban planning locking societies into carbon-intensive mobility patterns. Example: 'Sustainable transport options are often inaccessible or underfunded.'

Name: Corporate Influence & Lobbying
Description: Large corporations as major emitters and powerful political actors; lobbying, financial influence, and strategic communication (greenwashing) prioritising profits over climate action. Example: 'Greenwashing is constantly used by corporations to appear eco-friendly while continuing harmful practices.'

Name: Economic Growth
Description: Climate change as consequence of the capitalist model of endless economic growth driven by globalisation and industrialisation, prioritising GDP over ecological sustainability. Example: 'Infinite economic growth is incompatible with a finite planet.'

Name: Inequality & Environmental Injustice
Description: Unequal contributions to and impacts of climate change: wealthiest individuals and countries are the largest emitters, while the poorest face the most severe consequences. Example: 'The richest 1% are responsible for more emissions than the poorest 50%.'

Name: Scientific Weaponization
Description: Conspiracy theories suggesting scientific knowledge and technologies are manipulated for political, military, or corporate interests; climate change framed as a fabricated or engineered phenomenon. Example: 'Weather modification technologies (HAARP, chemtrails) are being used to engineer climate events.'

Name: Government Control
Description: Climate change portrayed as a pretext for increased government surveillance, regulation, and control over individual freedoms; fears of authoritarian agendas. Example: 'Climate change is a hoax designed to increase government control over personal freedoms.'

Name: Data Manipulation & Media Complicity
Description: Beliefs that scientific data is selectively presented, misinterpreted, or falsified; media complicit in spreading misleading or politically motivated information. Example: 'The media either overhypes or underreports climate change, leading to confusion.'

Name: Climate Change (Outcome)
Description: The terminal outcome node. All causal chains in the narrative ultimately lead to climate change. This node cannot be a source — only a target.
